name: Trinity nuclear test
summary: The first detonation of a nuclear weapon, in the New Mexico desert before dawn on 16 July 1945.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The product of the Manhattan Project, it made the [bombing of Hiroshima](event:hiroshima) possible three weeks later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test)).

name: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: Two atomic bombs killed well over 100,000 people; Japan surrendered within days.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). They remain the only use of nuclear weapons in war. The threat of their use structured the entire [Cold War](event:cold-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki).

name: Victory in Europe
summary: Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 7, ending the war in Europe and concluding the defeat of Nazi tyranny.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Germany's unconditional surrender was signed at Reims on 7 May and ratified in Berlin the next day. Hitler had killed himself a week earlier as Soviet troops fought through the capital.

Unlike the armistice that ended [the First World War](event:ww1), the surrender left no room to argue that Germany had not been beaten in the field. But victory in Europe was not peace: the continent was divided along the lines the armies had reached, and the wartime alliance dissolved into the [Cold War](event:cold-war) within two years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_in_Europe_Day).

name: Victory over Japan
summary: Japan surrendered on August 15, ending World War II and beginning the occupation of Japan that would remake East Asia.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, after the [atomic bombings](event:hiroshima) of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria; the formal instrument was signed aboard the USS Missouri on 2 September.

The Pacific war, which had begun with the attack on [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor), had lasted three years and eight months and cost millions of lives, most of them Chinese and Japanese civilians.

The American occupation that followed rewrote Japan's constitution, broke up the industrial combines and renounced war. The settlement held, though the bases on Okinawa remain contested.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_over_Japan_Day).

name: United Nations founded
summary: Fifty states signed the UN Charter in San Francisco, creating a permanent forum and a Security Council with teeth on paper.
body:
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights followed in 1948.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations).

name: Decolonisation
summary: Within thirty years of the Second World War, the European overseas empires dissolved into some seventy new states.
body:
It began with [India](event:indian-independence) in 1947 and accelerated through Africa after 1957; some transitions were negotiated, others — Algeria, Vietnam, Angola — were long wars.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization).

name: Independence of India and Pakistan
summary: Britain withdrew from South Asia, and the subcontinent was divided into two states.
body:
Part of [Decolonisation](event:decolonisation). Independence was the culmination of decades of mass campaigning, including [Gandhi's Salt March](event:salt-march). [Partition](event:partition) accompanied it: 10–20 million displaced and perhaps a million killed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement).

name: Partition of India
summary: Hastily drawn borders through Punjab and Bengal triggered the largest mass migration in history and appalling communal violence.
body:
Part of [Independence of India and Pakistan](event:indian-independence). Hastily drawn borders through Punjab and Bengal triggered the largest mass migration in history and appalling communal violence.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India).

name: The Cold War
summary: For forty-four years the United States and the Soviet Union confronted each other everywhere except in direct battle.
body:
It ran through the [Berlin blockade](event:berlin-blockade), [Korea](event:korean-war), the [Cuban Missile Crisis](event:cuban-missile-crisis) — the closest the world has come to nuclear war — [Vietnam](event:vietnam-war), and the [Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall).

It also drove the [Space Race](event:space-race). It ended with the [fall of the Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall) and the [collapse of the Soviet Union](event:soviet-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War).

name: Invention of the transistor
summary: Bell Labs built a solid-state amplifier and switch, the component from which all modern electronics is made.
body:
Shrinking transistors — from one per device to tens of billions on a [chip](event:microprocessor) — is the single trend behind computing, communications and the [internet](event:internet).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor).

name: Marshall Plan
summary: American aid worth some $13 billion rebuilt Western Europe's shattered economies and tied their recovery to an alliance with the United States.
body:
Proposed by Secretary of State George Marshall in June 1947 and enacted by Congress the following April, the European Recovery Program sent roughly $13 billion — over $150 billion in today's money — to sixteen countries over four years.

The aid revived industrial output and secured Western Europe's alignment with the United States during the [Cold War](event:cold-war). Its architects argued that rebuilding a defeated enemy worked better than the punitive settlement imposed after [the First World War](event:ww1).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan).

name: Founding of the State of Israel
summary: Israel declared independence as the British mandate ended; war with its Arab neighbours followed immediately, displacing some 700,000 Palestinians.
body:
Israel declared independence as the British mandate ended; war with its Arab neighbours followed immediately, displacing some 700,000 Palestinians.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Declaration_of_Independence).

name: Berlin Blockade and Airlift
summary: The Soviets cut off West Berlin; Allied aircraft supplied the city for eleven months.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Soviets cut off West Berlin; Allied aircraft supplied the city for eleven months.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Blockade).

name: NATO founded
summary: Twelve Western nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty, creating a collective-defence alliance that still stands today.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The treaty's Article 5 — that an attack on one is an attack on all — has been invoked only once, after [9/11](event:9-11). NATO expanded eastward after 1991, absorbing former Soviet satellite states and shaping European security for decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO).

name: People's Republic of China proclaimed
summary: Mao Zedong declared the PRC from Tiananmen after the Communist victory in the civil war.
body:
The following decades brought land reform, the famine of the Great Leap Forward, the [Cultural Revolution](event:cultural-revolution) and, after 1978, the reforms that made China the world's second-largest economy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China).

name: Korean War
summary: North Korean, Chinese, American and UN forces fought to a stalemate close to the original border; no peace treaty was ever signed.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). North Korean, Chinese, American and UN forces fought to a stalemate close to the original border; no peace treaty was ever signed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War).

name: Green Revolution
summary: High-yield dwarf wheat and rice, fertiliser and irrigation roughly tripled cereal yields in the developing world.
body:
Norman Borlaug's varieties are credited with averting famine for a billion people, at the cost of heavy fertiliser and water use.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution).

name: Structure of DNA
summary: Watson and Crick, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, described the double helix — and with it, how genes copy themselves.
body:
Molecular biology, genetic engineering, [the Human Genome Project](event:human-genome) and [CRISPR](event:crispr) all follow from this two-page paper.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleic_acid_double_helix).

name: American civil rights movement
summary: A mass campaign of boycotts, marches and litigation dismantled legal segregation in the United States.
body:
From *Brown v. Board* and the Montgomery bus boycott through the [March on Washington](event:march-washington) to the [Civil Rights Act](event:civil-rights-act) and the Voting Rights Act, and the [assassination of Martin Luther King](event:mlk-assassination).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement).

name: Polio vaccine developed
summary: Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine was declared safe and effective after the largest medical field trial ever run, and childhood polio soon vanished from the developed world.
body:
Polio had paralysed thousands of children each year; Salk's vaccine stopped the epidemics. Albert Sabin's live attenuated vaccine followed, leading to a global eradication campaign that nearly succeeded — only two endemic countries remain today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio_vaccine).

name: Vietnam War
summary: Two decades of war ended with American withdrawal and the unification of Vietnam under the north.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Perhaps three million Vietnamese died. Televised coverage and mass protest changed how Western democracies relate to their own wars.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War).

name: Suez Crisis
summary: Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal; Britain, France and Israel invaded; superpower pressure and humiliation forced withdrawal.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Egypt nationalised the canal in July 1956; Britain, France and Israel invaded in October under a secret plan. American financial pressure and Soviet threats forced a withdrawal within weeks.

The crisis ended Britain and France's standing as independent great powers in the Middle East and drew the region further into superpower competition.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis).

name: Hungarian Revolution
summary: Hungarians briefly freed themselves from Soviet control; Soviet tanks rolled in and crushed the uprising, killing thousands.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). A student demonstration in Budapest grew into a national uprising, and the new government of Imre Nagy declared neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact.

Soviet armour returned in early November. Some 2,500 Hungarians were killed, around 200,000 fled the country, and Nagy was executed two years later. The lesson — that Moscow would use force to hold its sphere — stood until the [Solidarity movement](event:solidarity-poland) tested it again.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1956).

name: The Space Race
summary: The superpowers competed to reach orbit, then the Moon, in a contest of prestige with military roots.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). It ran from [Sputnik](event:sputnik) through [Gagarin](event:gagarin) to the [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program), and ended symbolically with a US–Soviet docking in orbit in 1975.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race).

name: Sputnik 1
summary: The first artificial satellite beeped overhead every 96 minutes and stunned the United States into action.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). The first artificial satellite beeped overhead every 96 minutes and stunned the United States into action.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1).

name: Fidel Castro takes power in Cuba
summary: Castro's guerrillas overthrew the Batista regime; the revolution moved quickly leftward and allied with the Soviet Union.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The American embargo that followed pushed Cuba into Moscow's orbit and brought the superpowers perilously close to war at [the Cuban Missile Crisis](event:cuban-missile-crisis) three years later. Castro governed for nearly five decades, handing power to his brother in 2008.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Revolution).

name: Berlin Wall built
summary: East Germany walled off West Berlin overnight to stop the flight of its population.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). East Germany walled off West Berlin overnight to stop the flight of its population.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall).

name: Yuri Gagarin orbits the Earth
summary: The first human in space completed a single orbit aboard Vostok 1 and landed by parachute.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). The first human in space completed a single orbit aboard Vostok 1 and landed by parachute.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin).

name: Apollo programme
summary: Kennedy's commitment to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out mobilised 400,000 people and 4% of the federal budget.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). Kennedy's commitment to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out mobilised 400,000 people and 4% of the federal budget.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program).

name: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Thirteen days in October 1962 brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other moment.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Soviet missiles in Cuba were withdrawn in exchange for a US pledge not to invade and the quiet removal of American missiles from Turkey. A direct Moscow–Washington hotline followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis).

name: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
summary: President Kennedy was shot while riding through Dallas in an open car, and Vice-President Lyndon Johnson was sworn in the same afternoon.
body:
Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested and then shot dead two days later; the Warren Commission concluded he had acted alone, though doubts and conspiracy theories have never gone away.

The killing came between the [Cuban Missile Crisis](event:cuban-missile-crisis) and the escalation of [the Vietnam War](event:vietnam-war), and Johnson went on to sign the [Civil Rights Act](event:civil-rights-act) his predecessor had proposed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy).

name: March on Washington
summary: A quarter of a million people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to hear King's "I Have a Dream" speech.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). A quarter of a million people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to hear King's "I Have a Dream" speech.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Washington_for_Jobs_and_Freedom).

name: The Beatles rise to global fame
summary: Four Liverpool musicians from working-class families became the most popular band in the world, reshaping youth culture.
body:
Their appearance on American television in 1964 drew 73 million viewers. The Beatles pioneered album-focused releases, recording innovations, and psychedelic aesthetics, becoming the backdrop to the sixties counterculture and influencing music for generations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles).

name: Civil Rights Act of 1964
summary: Federal law outlawed discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin in employment and public accommodation.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). Federal law outlawed discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin in employment and public accommodation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964).

name: Cultural Revolution
summary: Mao mobilised students against the party and the "four olds"; universities closed, millions were persecuted and much cultural heritage was destroyed.
body:
Part of [People's Republic of China proclaimed](event:prc-founded). Mao mobilised students against the party and the "four olds"; universities closed, millions were persecuted and much cultural heritage was destroyed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution).

name: Six-Day War
summary: Israel decisively defeated Egypt, Syria and Jordan in six days, occupying the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Golan Heights.
body:
Israel opened the war with a pre-emptive air strike on Egypt and, within six days, held the Sinai, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.

The outcome left more than a million Palestinians under Israeli military occupation, a situation that has never been fully resolved. It reshaped the politics of the region and gave new impetus to the Palestinian national movement.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War).

name: First successful human heart transplant
summary: Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town transplanted a donor heart into a patient who survived for 18 days, proving transplantation possible.
body:
The patient, Louis Washkansky, lived nearly three weeks — long enough for the world to see that organ transplantation could work. The surgery sparked an international transplant race and led to today's routine organ and tissue replacements.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_transplantation).

name: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
summary: King was shot in Memphis while supporting a strike by sanitation workers; riots followed in over a hundred cities.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). King was shot in Memphis while supporting a strike by sanitation workers; riots followed in over a hundred cities.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr.).

name: Stonewall uprising
summary: Police raided a gay bar in Greenwich Village; the community fought back, sparking the modern LGBTQ rights movement.
body:
Police raids on gay bars were routine; on this night the crowd at the Stonewall Inn fought back, and the confrontation ran over several nights in Greenwich Village.

The first Pride marches were held on its anniversary a year later. The movement that grew from it won decriminalisation and, in much of the West, formal equality — including [marriage rights in the United States](event:usa-marriage-equality) in 2015.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_riots).

name: The Troubles begin in Northern Ireland
summary: Civil rights marches by Northern Ireland’s Catholic minority met violence, and the province slid into three decades of sectarian conflict.
body:
Rioting in Derry and Belfast in August 1969 brought British troops onto the streets. The Provisional IRA and loyalist paramilitaries fought a long campaign of shootings and bombings against each other, the security forces and civilians.

Around 3,500 people were killed, more than half of them civilians, before [the Good Friday Agreement](event:good-friday-agreement) of 1998 brought the conflict to an end.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles).

name: Apollo 11 Moon landing
summary: Humans walked on another world for the first time; some 600 million people watched.
body:
Part of [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program). *That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.* Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 hours on the Sea of Tranquillity while Collins orbited above.

It was the culmination of the [Space Race](event:space-race), and the furthest humans have yet travelled.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11).

image.caption: Buzz Aldrin on the lunar surface

name: ARPANET and the Internet
summary: The first packet-switched network linked four American universities; TCP/IP made networks of networks possible.
body:
It carried email, then the [World Wide Web](event:www), and now most of human communication and commerce.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET).

name: Apollo 13
summary: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon; the crew improvised their way home in the lunar module.
body:
Part of [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program). An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon; the crew improvised their way home in the lunar module.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13).

name: The microprocessor
summary: Intel put a whole central processing unit on one chip, making computers cheap enough to be everywhere.
body:
Part of [Invention of the transistor](event:transistor). Intel put a whole central processing unit on one chip, making computers cheap enough to be everywhere.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprocessor).

name: Watergate scandal
summary: A burglary at Democratic Party headquarters in Washington unravelled into a scandal that forced Richard Nixon to resign, the only US president ever to do so.
body:
Congressional hearings and press reporting traced the break-in of June 1972 back to the White House, exposing wiretapping, hush money and obstruction of justice. Nixon resigned in August 1974 rather than face impeachment.

The affair produced a wave of reform — campaign finance limits, the Ethics in Government Act, a stronger Freedom of Information Act — and a durable public distrust of the presidency.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal).

name: 1973 oil crisis
summary: Arab oil producers embargoed the West over its support for Israel; oil prices quadrupled and shortages wracked the developed world.
body:
Western economies relied on cheap oil; the embargo showed their vulnerability and sparked the first energy crisis. It prompted a shift toward nuclear power, fuel efficiency and eventually renewable energy development.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis).

name: Soweto uprising
summary: School students in Soweto marched against compulsory teaching in Afrikaans; police opened fire, and the killings turned a protest into a national revolt against apartheid.
body:
Estimates of the dead range from the official figure of 176 to several hundred. Photographs of the shootings circulated worldwide and hardened international opinion against the South African government.

A generation radicalised by Soweto sustained the resistance through the 1980s, on the road that led to [the end of apartheid](event:apartheid-end).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_uprising).

name: Voyager probes launched
summary: Two spacecraft toured the outer planets and are now the most distant human-made objects, in interstellar space.
body:
Two spacecraft toured the outer planets and are now the most distant human-made objects, in interstellar space.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_program).

name: Camp David Accords
summary: Egypt and Israel agreed a framework for peace after thirteen days of talks at the US presidential retreat, leading to a treaty signed the following year.
body:
President Carter mediated between Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin; the accords led to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty of 1979, the first between Israel and an Arab state, and the return of the Sinai to Egypt.

Sadat was widely condemned in the Arab world and was assassinated in 1981, but the treaty has held for more than four decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_David_Accords).

name: Iranian Revolution
summary: The shah was overthrown; Ayatollah Khomeini led an Islamic revolution that transformed Iran and reshaped the Middle East.
body:
Mass strikes and street protests forced Mohammad Reza Shah into exile in January 1979; Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile weeks later, and a referendum established an Islamic republic.

The revolution inspired Islamist political movements across the region and turned Iran from an American ally into an adversary. The hostage crisis at the US embassy, the war with Iraq and decades of confrontation followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution).

name: Three Mile Island nuclear accident
summary: A stuck valve and misread instruments led to a partial meltdown at a Pennsylvania reactor, the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power.
body:
Roughly half the reactor core melted, but the containment building held and measured radiation doses to the surrounding population were small. An advisory to pregnant women and small children prompted some 140,000 people to leave the area.

The accident was far smaller than [Chernobyl](event:chernobyl) seven years later, but it shattered American confidence in nuclear power: new reactor orders effectively stopped for three decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Mile_Island_accident).

name: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: Soviet troops invaded to prop up a faltering communist regime; a decade-long war and insurgency followed, draining the USSR.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Soviet forces entered in December 1979 to prop up a communist government losing control of the countryside, and stayed for nine years.

The United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan armed and funded the mujahideen. Around a million Afghans died and millions more became refugees. The withdrawal in 1989 damaged the Soviet leadership's authority on the eve of [the union's collapse](event:soviet-collapse), and left Afghanistan in a civil war from which the Taliban emerged.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War).

name: Solidarity movement emerges in Poland
summary: Trade unionists led by Lech Walesa organised strikes and protests against communist rule; the movement eventually brought down the regime.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Strikes at the Gdansk shipyard produced the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, led by the electrician Lech Walesa; within a year it claimed ten million members.

Martial law drove it underground in 1981, but it survived. Round-table talks in 1989 led to partly free elections that Solidarity won overwhelmingly — the opening move in the year that ended with [the fall of the Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union)).

name: Eradication of smallpox
summary: The WHO declared smallpox eradicated — the only human disease ever deliberately eliminated.
body:
A worldwide campaign of surveillance and ring [vaccination](event:smallpox-vaccine) ended a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox).

name: AIDS epidemic identified
summary: US doctors reported clusters of rare infections in previously healthy young men, the first recognition of the disease later named AIDS.
body:
The virus behind it, HIV, was identified in 1983. Spreading through blood and sexual contact, the epidemic had killed an estimated 40 million people worldwide by the early 2020s, with sub-Saharan Africa worst affected.

Antiretroviral drugs from 1996 turned the infection into a manageable chronic condition where they were available. The epidemic reshaped public health practice, drug regulation and patient activism.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS).

name: Falkland Islands War
summary: Argentina invaded the British Falkland Islands; Britain retook them in a ten-week war fought thousands of miles from Europe.
body:
Argentina's military government seized the islands in April 1982; Britain sent a naval task force 8,000 miles south and retook them by mid-June. Some 650 Argentine and 255 British personnel died, along with three islanders.

Defeat discredited the Argentine junta, which fell within a year, while the victory strengthened Margaret Thatcher's government in Britain.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War).

name: Chernobyl disaster
summary: A reactor test went catastrophically wrong, spreading radioactive fallout across Europe and forcing permanent evacuation.
body:
The accident damaged Soviet credibility at home and abroad and reshaped nuclear policy worldwide.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernobyl_disaster).

name: Montreal Protocol
summary: Every country agreed to phase out CFCs to protect the ozone layer — the most successful environmental treaty yet made.
body:
The ozone hole is now measurably healing, and the treaty avoided a great deal of additional [warming](event:global-warming) as well.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Protocol).

name: Tiananmen Square protests
summary: Students and workers occupied the centre of Beijing for seven weeks demanding reform; the army cleared the square by force, killing hundreds or more.
body:
The protests spread to cities across China and were the largest challenge the Communist Party had faced since the [Cultural Revolution](event:cultural-revolution). Martial law was declared and troops moved in on the night of 3 June.

Death tolls remain disputed: official figures cite around 200, while other estimates run into the thousands. The crackdown brought international sanctions and ended a decade of political liberalisation, though economic reform continued.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre).

name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: A confused press conference on 9 November sent crowds to the checkpoints, and the guards let them through.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Within a year Germany was reunified; within two the [Soviet Union](event:soviet-collapse) had dissolved. Communist governments across Eastern Europe fell in the same few months.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall).

name: World Wide Web
summary: Tim Berners-Lee proposed a hypertext system at CERN; it became the way most of humanity gets information.
body:
URLs, HTTP and HTML were released royalty-free in 1993, a decision that let the Web grow without a gatekeeper. Built on the [Internet](event:internet), it took the number of connected users from thousands to billions in two decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web).

name: Reunification of Germany
summary: East and West Germany merged less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell, reuniting a nation divided for forty-five years.
body:
The [fall of the Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall) was followed by free elections in the east and a treaty settlement with the four wartime occupying powers. Reunification took formal effect on 3 October 1990.

Integration was swift but costly: eastern industry collapsed and regional disparities persist. Reunified Germany became the anchor of the [European Union](event:maastricht) and Europe's largest economy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification).

name: Breakup of Yugoslavia
summary: Yugoslavia fragmented into separate states, and the wars that followed brought the worst violence in Europe since 1945.
body:
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in June 1991, followed by Macedonia and Bosnia. The federal army and Serb paramilitaries fought to hold territory; the wars in Croatia and Bosnia brought sieges, mass expulsions and the massacre of some 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in 1995.

Around 130,000 people died and millions were displaced. The conflicts produced the first international war crimes tribunal since Nuremberg and reshaped European security policy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia).

name: First Gulf War
summary: Iraq annexed Kuwait in 1990; a US-led coalition authorised by the UN drove its forces out in six weeks of air and ground warfare.
body:
Operation Desert Storm began in January 1991 with a five-week air campaign, followed by a ground offensive that ended in a hundred hours. Coalition losses were light; Iraqi military and civilian deaths ran to tens of thousands, and retreating troops set fire to Kuwait's oil wells.

The war confirmed American military primacy at the close of the [Cold War](event:cold-war). Sanctions, no-fly zones and a continued US military presence in the Gulf followed, and Saddam Hussein remained in power until [2003](event:iraq-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War).

name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The USSR broke into fifteen independent states and the Cold War ended without a shot fired between the superpowers.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Gorbachev's reforms, nationalist movements in the republics and a failed hard-line coup in August 1991 brought down the state founded by the [October Revolution](event:october-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union).

name: Maastricht Treaty and the European Union
summary: The European Communities became the European Union, with a common currency to follow in 1999.
body:
The European Communities became the European Union, with a common currency to follow in 1999.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty).

name: Rwandan genocide
summary: Some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were murdered in a hundred days while the world looked away.
body:
Some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were murdered in a hundred days while the world looked away.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide).

name: End of apartheid in South Africa
summary: Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for 27 years, was elected president in the country's first universal-suffrage election.
body:
The negotiated transition and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission avoided the civil war many had predicted.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid).

name: Dolly the sheep cloned
summary: Scottish scientists cloned an adult sheep using nuclear transfer, proving that the genome of an adult cell could be reprogrammed.
body:
Dolly was born at the Roslin Institute in July 1996 and announced to the world the following February. She was created by transferring the nucleus of an adult mammary cell into an emptied egg.

The result overturned the assumption that specialised adult cells could not be reset, opening the way to stem-cell reprogramming and regenerative medicine, and prompting immediate debate about human cloning.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_(sheep)).

name: Kyoto Protocol signed
summary: Industrialised nations accepted binding limits on greenhouse gas emissions, the first treaty to put numbers on climate commitments.
body:
The protocol bound developed countries to cut emissions below 1990 levels while exempting developing ones — a division that led the United States to sign but never ratify. It entered force in 2005 once Russia ratified.

Global emissions kept rising, and the successor [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) of 2015 replaced binding targets with national pledges. Both are responses to [modern global warming](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol).

name: Good Friday Agreement
summary: Ireland and Britain signed an agreement ending 30 years of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland, establishing a power-sharing government.
body:
Part of the settlement of [the Troubles](event:troubles-begin). Multi-party talks produced power-sharing institutions in Belfast, cross-border bodies with the Republic, and provisions for prisoner release and paramilitary disarmament.

Voters on both sides of the border approved it by referendum. Devolved government has been suspended several times since, and [Brexit](event:brexit-referendum) reopened the question of the Irish border, but the peace has held.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday_Agreement).

name: War in Afghanistan begins
summary: The US and NATO invaded Afghanistan to overthrow the Taliban and crush al-Qaeda, beginning a twenty-year occupation.
body:
Part of the response to [9/11](event:9-11). A US-led campaign with Afghan allies removed the Taliban government within weeks, but Osama bin Laden escaped and the insurgency regrouped.

Twenty years of occupation and state-building followed, at a cost of some 170,000 lives. NATO forces withdrew in 2021 and the Taliban retook Kabul within days.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021)).

name: September 11 attacks
summary: Hijacked airliners destroyed the World Trade Center and struck the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people.
body:
The attacks triggered the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, a global expansion of surveillance, and two decades of security policy still in force.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks).

name: Invasion of Iraq
summary: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq on the claim that it held weapons of mass destruction; none were found, and the occupation destabilised the region for years.
body:
Baghdad fell in three weeks and Saddam Hussein's government collapsed, but the occupation met a growing insurgency and a sectarian civil war. Estimates of the dead range from around 200,000 documented civilian deaths to survey figures several times higher.

The war divided the Western alliance, drew the largest anti-war protests in decades, and left a weakened Iraqi state in which the Islamic State later took root.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq).

name: Human Genome Project completed
summary: Thirteen years and three billion base pairs later, the human genetic sequence was published and placed in the public domain.
body:
Sequencing a genome cost about a billion dollars in 2003 and a few hundred today — one of the fastest cost collapses in the history of technology. See also [CRISPR](event:crispr).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Genome_Project).

name: Facebook founded
summary: Mark Zuckerberg launched a social network from his Harvard dorm; it grew to billions of users and reshaped how humans communicate.
body:
Started as a network for Harvard students, Facebook opened to the public in 2006 and passed a billion users in 2012, absorbing Instagram and WhatsApp along the way.

It made social networking the dominant form of online communication and advertising the dominant business model of the web. It also became the focus of arguments over privacy, algorithmic amplification, misinformation and the effects of social media on adolescents.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook).

name: Hurricane Katrina
summary: A hurricane that had peaked at Category 5 over the Gulf came ashore as a Category 3 and breached the levees protecting New Orleans, flooding most of the city.
body:
More than 1,800 people died and over a million were displaced across the Gulf coast. Water covered around 80 per cent of New Orleans for weeks, and the failure of the federal and local relief effort became a national scandal.

The flooding fell hardest on the city's poorest neighbourhoods, and the storm became a reference point in arguments about extreme weather under [modern global warming](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina).

name: The smartphone era
summary: The iPhone put a networked computer with a camera in a pocket, and within a decade most of humanity carried one.
body:
The iPhone put a networked computer with a camera in a pocket, and within a decade most of humanity carried one.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_(1st_generation)).

name: Barack Obama elected president
summary: Obama became the first African-American US president, amid the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.
body:
Obama won the presidency in the weeks after the [financial crisis](event:financial-crisis) broke, becoming the first African-American to hold the office.

His two terms brought a health insurance expansion, the nuclear agreement with Iran and the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) on climate. He faced sustained congressional opposition, and much of the programme was reversed by his successor.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama).

name: Global financial crisis
summary: The collapse of the American mortgage market brought down banks worldwide and caused the deepest recession since the 1930s.
body:
The collapse of the American mortgage market brought down banks worldwide and caused the deepest recession since the 1930s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007–2008_financial_crisis).

name: Arab Spring
summary: Protests spread from Tunisia across the Arab world, toppling four governments and setting off civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen.
body:
Protests spread from Tunisia across the Arab world, toppling four governments and setting off civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Spring).

name: Fukushima nuclear disaster
summary: An earthquake and tsunami knocked out cooling at a Japanese nuclear plant, and three reactor cores melted down in the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl.
body:
The tsunami that caused the accident killed around 18,000 people along the coast. The meltdowns themselves caused no immediate radiation deaths, but forced the evacuation of some 150,000 people, and more than 2,000 later deaths have been attributed to the strain of displacement.

Japan shut down its reactor fleet and Germany announced a nuclear phase-out — a setback for low-carbon generation at a critical point in the response to [global warming](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_nuclear_accident).

name: Curiosity rover lands on Mars
summary: A one-tonne rover touched down in Gale Crater to explore whether Mars ever harboured life, beginning the most ambitious planetary survey yet.
body:
Launched from Cape Canaveral in November 2011, the one-tonne rover was lowered into Gale Crater by a rocket-powered sky crane in August 2012.

Curiosity has outlasted its two-year primary mission many times over, finding ancient lakebed sediments and organic molecules that show Mars was once warmer, wetter and potentially habitable.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_(rover)).

name: Discovery of the Higgs boson
summary: The LHC at CERN found the particle that completes the Standard Model and explains how other particles acquire mass.
body:
The LHC at CERN found the particle that completes the Standard Model and explains how other particles acquire mass.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson).

name: CRISPR gene editing
summary: A bacterial immune system was turned into a cheap, precise tool for editing the DNA of any organism.
body:
Doudna and Charpentier shared the 2020 Nobel Prize; the first approved CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease, arrived in 2023. See [DNA](event:dna-structure).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR_gene_editing).

name: Deep learning and modern AI
summary: Neural networks trained on large datasets went from academic curiosity to general-purpose technology in about a decade.
body:
AlexNet's 2012 win in an image-recognition contest started the boom; transformer models from 2017 led to systems that write, translate, code and reason across domains.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning).

name: Edward Snowden reveals NSA mass surveillance
summary: A former NSA contractor, speaking from Hong Kong, gave journalists documents showing that US and allied agencies collected phone and internet records on a mass scale.
body:
The disclosures described bulk telephone metadata collection, access to the records of major internet services and the tapping of undersea cables. Snowden was charged under the Espionage Act and took refuge in Russia.

The revelations forced a public argument about surveillance and civil liberties, prompted limited legal reform in the United States, and pushed the technology industry to encrypt traffic by default.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden).

name: Same-sex marriage legalized in the US
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry, following decades of activism and court battles.
body:
Obergefell v. Hodges held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires states to license and recognise marriages between same-sex couples, settling the question across all fifty states.

The decision came less than fifty years after [the Stonewall uprising](event:stonewall-uprising), and followed a rapid shift in public opinion. Marriage equality has since been adopted in more than thirty countries, while same-sex relationships remain criminalised in many others.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obergefell_v._Hodges).

name: First detection of gravitational waves
summary: LIGO recorded spacetime ripples from two merging black holes, a century after [Einstein](event:relativity) predicted them.
body:
LIGO recorded spacetime ripples from two merging black holes, a century after [Einstein](event:relativity) predicted them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_observation_of_gravitational_waves).

name: Paris Agreement on climate change
summary: Nearly every country agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C, with national pledges rather than binding quotas.
body:
It is the main international response to [modern global warming](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement).

name: Brexit referendum
summary: British voters chose to leave the European Union by a narrow margin, triggering a constitutional crisis and reshaping European politics.
body:
Fifty-two per cent voted to leave, on a turnout of seventy-two. The result reflected long-running arguments over sovereignty, immigration and the distribution of the gains from globalisation.

The United Kingdom left the [European Union](event:maastricht) in 2020 after four years of negotiation. Trade frictions followed, and the vote strained the union between England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, where it reopened questions settled by [the Good Friday Agreement](event:good-friday-agreement).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit).

name: MeToo movement emerges
summary: Women shared stories of sexual harassment and assault on social media, sparking a global reckoning with gender violence and workplace abuse.
body:
The phrase, coined by the activist Tarana Burke in 2006, spread worldwide after allegations against the film producer Harvey Weinstein were published in October 2017.

The movement led to prosecutions and resignations across entertainment, media, politics and business, and to revised workplace conduct rules. It also prompted argument about due process and about how allegations should be handled.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Me_Too_movement).

name: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A novel coronavirus spread worldwide within months, killing an estimated 7–27 million people and shutting down much of the global economy.
body:
It produced the fastest vaccine development in history: mRNA vaccines were in arms within a year of the virus being sequenced. Comparisons were drawn throughout to the [1918 influenza pandemic](event:spanish-flu).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic).

name: James Webb Space Telescope
summary: A 6.5-metre infrared telescope launched to a point 1.5 million km from Earth to observe the first galaxies.
body:
A 6.5-metre infrared telescope launched to a point 1.5 million km from Earth to observe the first galaxies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope).

name: ChatGPT released
summary: OpenAI released a conversational interface to a large language model; it reached a hundred million users within two months and made generative AI a mass technology.
body:
The system built on the transformer architecture and the [deep learning](event:deep-learning) methods of the previous decade, but its chat interface put them in ordinary hands for the first time.

Its release set off a wave of investment and competition, and arguments over copyright, misinformation, the future of skilled work and the governance of increasingly capable systems.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT).

name: Russian invasion of Ukraine
summary: Russia launched the largest land war in Europe since 1945, driving millions from their homes and reshaping European security.
body:
Russia launched the largest land war in Europe since 1945, driving millions from their homes and reshaping European security.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine).

name: World population reaches 8 billion
summary: The UN marked an eightfold increase in human numbers since 1800, with growth now slowing worldwide.
body:
The UN marked an eightfold increase in human numbers since 1800, with growth now slowing worldwide.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population).

name: Israel-Hamas war begins
summary: Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking some 250 hostages; Israel responded with an air and ground campaign in Gaza.
body:
The attack of 7 October 2023 was the deadliest day for Israelis since the state was founded. The Israeli campaign that followed killed tens of thousands of Palestinians according to Gaza health authorities, displaced most of the territory's population and left much of it in ruins.

The war brought accusations of war crimes against both sides before international courts, protests worldwide, and fighting that drew in armed groups in Lebanon and Yemen as well as Iran.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war).

name: Turkey-Syria earthquake
summary: A 7.8 magnitude earthquake killed over 50,000 in Turkey and Syria, one of the deadliest earthquakes in a century.
body:
The magnitude 7.8 shock struck before dawn near Gaziantep and was followed hours later by a second of magnitude 7.5. Around 60,000 people were killed and millions were left homeless.

Poorly enforced building codes explained much of the collapse in Turkey, while in northern Syria a decade of war had already destroyed housing and hampered the relief effort.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Turkey%E2%80%93Syria_earthquakes).
